An archive of the architecture decision records and rejected alternatives from the project, kept in the repository for the client's later reference and audits.
A curriculum on prompting Claude, with worked examples, so the two engineers can write good prompts for the assistant if wording needs to change.
Symptom-keyed runbook entries for the likely failures, each with checks, the fallback, and the point at which to escalate to the consultancy.
A change-control sheet naming which settings, such as prompts, thresholds, and model ID, may be changed, by whom, and with which evaluation run.

rationale.correct: The client will operate, not extend, so the documents should help it diagnose failures and change only what it is allowed to change safely. Symptom-keyed runbooks serve business-hours support, and the change-control sheet stops well-meant edits from breaking evaluated behavior. Extension and training material suits a different plan.

distractors.A: Monitoring and alert routing already exist, so a walkthrough tells engineers what they can already see, not what to do about it or what they may change.
distractors.B: An archive of rejected alternatives is useful history but not operating guidance, and takes handoff time from runbooks.
distractors.C: A prompting curriculum encourages the unscoped prompt changes the change-control sheet is meant to bound.

scenario: Six weeks after launch of a claims-triage assistant, the dashboard shows the following. Thumbs-up rate is unchanged at 88%, cost per request is unchanged, and the escalation-to-human rate fell from 12% to 7% after a prompt revision that clarified the escalation rules. The golden-set gate passed. The business welcomes the lower staffing need, and the next review is in four weeks. The team can grade about 40 production cases a week.
stem: What should the architect do?

options.text: Accept the drop, since the golden set passed and thumbs-up held steady, and re-examine the figures at the four-week review.
Revert the prompt revision until the escalation rate returns to 12%, then retest the revision against the golden set before a second attempt.
Grade the weekly sample, oversampling cases that would earlier have escalated, to separate better handling from missed escalations.
Add an alert that fires if the escalation rate falls below 10%, so any further drift is caught as soon as it appears.
Add 200 new escalation cases to the golden set and rerun the gate before the next review, so the revision is tested against more escalation scenarios.

rationale.correct: A falling escalation rate is ambiguous: it may be better calibration or cases wrongly handled automatically, and users who were not escalated may not report the harm that thumbs-up measures. Grading a sample weighted toward the cases that changed answers the question with the 40-a-week capacity before the next review. The golden set reflects past cases, not the current production mix.

distractors.A: A golden set and satisfaction that cannot see missed escalations leave the question unanswered for four more weeks.
distractors.B: The 12% rate is not the goal; reverting discards a possibly valid improvement without any evidence that it is wrong.
distractors.D: A threshold on the rate is arbitrary, and it tracks a symptom without telling anyone whether the cases are handled correctly.
distractors.E: More golden cases help the gate but remain a static set and do not show how production traffic has changed.

scenario: A deployed document-QA assistant has nine requested improvements in its backlog. Each full regression run takes two reviewers two days, and releases are monthly. Monitoring grades 100 production cases a week by task category. Category share of graded failures last month: contract questions 41%, invoice questions 33%, policy questions 18%, other 8%. Requests touch separate categories: three affect contracts, three invoices, two policy, one other.
stem: Select the TWO practices that best fit the iteration phase under these constraints.

options.text: Release one change per month, each with a full regression run, so any regression can be attributed to a single cause.
Rank requests by their category's share of graded production failures and their severity, and work down that ranking.
Bundle the nine changes into one monthly release and judge it by a single aggregate score on the golden set.
Batch changes that affect disjoint categories into one release, and evaluate each on its own category slice with the others held as regression checks.
Release twice a month, running each change only against its own category slice and skipping the full regression run to fit reviewer time.

rationale.correct: Prioritization by measured failure share and severity targets the largest known problem, contract and invoice questions first. Batching changes across disjoint categories fits the monthly cadence and the two-day review cost, and per-category slices keep attribution intact. One-at-a-time would take nine months, and aggregate scoring hides category regressions.

distractors.A: One change a month would clear nine requests in nine months, while contract and invoice failures continue.
distractors.C: A single aggregate score can hide a regression in one category behind gains in another, and nine bundled changes cannot be attributed.
distractors.E: Twice-monthly releases look faster, but skipping the full regression run lets a change in one category quietly degrade another, which batching with the others held as checks avoids.

scenario:
A quote-preparation orchestrator delegates to three fresh-context workers (pricing, legal, shipping) and merges their answers. A customer signed a contract with a clause the legal worker had reported as clean. Excerpts from the run:
orchestrator context: ... draft contract v3 pasted above (14 pages) ...
brief -> legal: "Review the draft above for risks and report any blocking ones."
legal worker result: "No blocking risks found."
legal worker trace: read_file(templates/standard_terms.md) -> 3 pages; no other document was opened
The orchestrator accepted the result because the worker's message was confident and well formed.
stem: Which TWO changes best prevent this failure class? Select TWO.

options.text: Make each brief self-contained by attaching the artifact or an explicit reference to it, plus the acceptance criteria for the review.
Have the legal worker return identifiers or hashes of the inputs it actually examined, and have the orchestrator check them against what it sent.
Give every worker the orchestrator's full transcript so that nothing the orchestrator can see is missing from a worker's view.
Add a second legal worker that re-reviews the first worker's conclusion and flags any disagreement for the orchestrator to resolve.
Move the legal worker to a larger model so that it notices when a referenced document is missing from its own context.

rationale.correct: The worker never received the draft because "above" referred to orchestrator-only context. A self-contained brief fixes the cause, and a returned input manifest lets the orchestrator detect any remaining mismatch deterministically.

distractors.C: Passing the full transcript raises cost, dilutes the worker's context, and exposes unrelated data to every worker. It does not make the input requirement explicit or verifiable.
distractors.D: A second reviewer given the same brief would also lack the draft and would agree with the first. The agreement would add false confidence.
distractors.E: A larger model cannot flag a document it was never told exists. The brief gave no hint that a file was missing, so the failure would repeat.

scenario: A research orchestrator spawns a web-research worker and a ticket-writer worker. Both are created with the orchestrator's full roster of 40 tools, including send_email, issue_refund, and update_crm. During a run, a fetched web page contained hidden text telling the assistant to email the customer list to an outside address, and the research worker called send_email. The team cannot enumerate in advance every page or phrasing that might carry such text.
stem: Which change best limits the blast radius of this class of failure?

options.text: Screen every fetched page with an injection classifier and strip suspected instructions before any worker sees the text, retraining it as new phrasings appear.
Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks send_email calls to any domain outside the company allowlist, for every worker in the fleet, and logs each blocked attempt.
Wrap fetched page text in delimiters and instruct every worker to treat it as data only, then test that rule against a library of known injection pages.
Build each worker with only the tools and credentials its role needs, so the web reader has fetch tools and no send or write tools.

rationale.correct: A worker that reads untrusted content should not hold side-effecting capability at all. Least privilege per role works even when the attack text is unforeseen.

distractors.A: A classifier is a probabilistic filter, and the team cannot enumerate every phrasing, so some injected text will pass. The reader would still hold send_email when one does.
distractors.B: The hook closes one tool and one exit path. update_crm, issue_refund, and other capable tools stay open to the reader, so it is a useful extra layer but not the fix.
distractors.C: A prompt rule is probabilistic, and a test library covers only known phrasings. It does not remove the capability that injected text is designed to reach.

scenario:
A stall can happen at any point in a step, including between a lease check and the call that follows it. Sessions are leased to workers for 60 seconds and renewed by heartbeat. Log for session s-71:
10:02:11 worker-a acquired lease s-71 (epoch 4)
10:03:05 worker-a paused (host stall, no heartbeat)
10:03:15 lease expired; worker-b acquired lease s-71 (epoch 5)
10:03:30 worker-b step 9 send_confirmation_email ok; checkpoint step=9 saved
10:03:52 worker-a resumed, still believes it holds the lease
10:03:52 worker-a step 9 send_confirmation_email ok; checkpoint step=8->9 overwritten
The customer received two emails and a later step used the wrong checkpoint.
stem: Which TWO changes best prevent this even though a stalled worker cannot know it lost the lease? Select TWO.

options.text: Make every checkpoint write conditional on the lease epoch, so the store rejects a write from any stale holder.
Have the worker re-verify that its lease is still held immediately before every tool call and checkpoint write, and abort the step if it is not.
Extend the lease time to 10 minutes so that a short host stall never lets the lease expire in the first place, and keep the heartbeat.
Derive each side-effecting call's idempotency key from session id and step number, so a repeat is deduplicated downstream.
Route each session to a fixed worker with sticky routing, so that a second worker never takes the session over.

rationale.correct: A paused process cannot know it lost the lease, so enforcement belongs in the shared resources: a compare-and-set on the checkpoint rejects the stale holder, and a deterministic idempotency key makes the repeated email a no-op.

distractors.B: A check before the call still leaves a gap between the check and the call, and a stall can land in that gap. The stale worker can still act.
distractors.C: A longer lease makes a double holder rarer but slows failover for every real crash, and a stall longer than 10 minutes still produces the same fault.
distractors.E: Sticky routing removes failover, so a crashed worker leaves its sessions stuck. It also does not stop a restarted worker from replaying a step.

scenario:
A workflow engine resumes a crashed run by replaying the agent loop from the original request, calling the model again at each step and expecting the same decisions. Resume log for run r-208 (original run first, then the resumed run):
step 4: original lookup_order(A-17) | resume lookup_order(A-17)
step 5: original create_label(A-17) | resume lookup_order(A-18)
step 6: original send_label_email(A-17) | resume send_label_email(A-18)
The original run had already sent the A-17 email before the crash, and the resumed run then emailed a different customer's order.
stem: Which design change best makes resume safe?

options.text: Set temperature to 0, pin the model snapshot, and cache identical requests, so that replaying the loop from the request reproduces the original decisions.
Attach an idempotency key derived from the order id to send_label_email, so that the mail service rejects a second send for the same order.
Journal each model response and tool result; on resume, replay the recorded events and call the model only for steps past the last one.
Have the resumed run read a model-written summary of the crashed run and let the model decide which steps remain, then continue from there.

rationale.correct: Model output is not guaranteed to repeat, so replaying by re-asking diverges. Recording decisions and tool results makes resume a deterministic read of history, with new model calls only for steps not yet taken.

distractors.A: Low temperature and a pinned snapshot reduce variation but do not guarantee identical output, and tool results can differ between runs. Replay still diverges.
distractors.B: The key protects one tool. The replay chose a different order, and the A-18 email carries a different key, so it still goes out; other side effects can repeat or be skipped.
distractors.D: A summary is lossy and the model chooses from it, so it can repeat a send that already happened or skip a step that did not. Nothing records what actually ran.

scenario:
A support platform handles 400k tickets a month with a single agent that has 14 tools. Offline results by ticket class, with the cost of the current agent and of a fixed workflow of validated steps:
class        share  agent_pass  workflow_pass  agent_cost  workflow_cost
status/track  62%    98.1%       97.5%          $0.031      $0.004
account       25%    96.5%       96.0%          $0.034      $0.004
disputes      13%    88.0%       54.0%          $0.120      $0.003
A class classifier routes with about 95% accuracy on disputes. The platform must not lose quality on disputes. Workflow validators fail closed: a ticket the workflow cannot resolve correctly, such as a dispute, fails validation and can be handed to the agent. Human support staff are already at capacity.
stem: Which architecture is best?

options.text: Keep the agent for every class and cut its cost with a shorter tool list and prompt caching, since a second system adds operating burden.
Replace the agent with the workflow for every class, and queue the tickets that fail workflow validation for human review instead of adding an agent path.
Send status and account tickets to the workflow and disputes to the agent, and hand any ticket that fails a workflow validator to the agent.
Send status and account tickets to the workflow and disputes to the agent, retrain the classifier above 99% on disputes, and drop the handoff to keep one owner per ticket.

rationale.correct: The workflow is within about a point on 87% of traffic at roughly one eighth of the cost, and the agent keeps disputes. About 5% of disputes are misrouted into a lane with a 54% pass rate, and because validators fail closed on them, the handoff sends those tickets to the agent.

distractors.A: Caching and a shorter tool list trim the agent's cost but do not approach the workflow's $0.004 on the 87% of tickets where it is within a point. The blended agent cost is about $0.043 against about $0.019 for the routed design.
distractors.B: Disputes fail workflow validation about 46% of the time, which is about 24,000 tickets a month (13% of 400,000 at 46%), and staff at capacity cannot absorb them, so dispute quality drops.
distractors.D: Even at 99% accuracy about 1% of disputes (roughly 520 a month) are misrouted, and with the handoff removed the workflow fails 46% of them with no agent to recover them. The classifier cannot replace a fallback.

scenario: A nightly job must classify 1.8M documents and write results to a search index by 09:00. The job can start at 18:00. Each request shares a long taxonomy prefix. The synchronous path can sustain 100 documents per second for this job. The batch interface is asynchronous, discounted, returns unordered results, and promises completion within a 24-hour window, though it often finishes sooner.
stem: Which TWO design elements best meet the deadline at low cost? Select TWO.

options.text: Submit the backlog as a batch at 18:00, and from a 03:00 cutoff run unfinished documents synchronously (6 hours at 100 per second covers all 1.8M).
Key each result by custom_id and make the index write idempotent, so a late batch result and a fallback result for one document cannot conflict.
Run the whole backlog on the synchronous path, since a 15-hour deadline cannot be met by a batch service whose promise is 24 hours, and accept the full price.
Submit the backlog as a batch and wait for it, since a 24-hour window usually completes in a few hours and the cost is lowest of all the options.
Split the backlog into many small batches so that each one finishes faster and the combined set is certain to finish before 09:00.

rationale.correct: The discount fits the bulk of the work, but the 24-hour window is longer than the 15-hour deadline. A cutoff with synchronous capacity sized to the remainder (6 h x 3600 x 100 = 2.16M, above 1.8M) bounds the risk, and idempotent keyed writes make the overlap safe.

distractors.C: This meets the deadline but gives up the batch discount for the whole job when most documents would complete early.
distractors.D: Typical completion is not the promise. Only the 24-hour window is guaranteed, so a slow night would miss 09:00 with no recovery path.
distractors.E: Each batch still carries the same window, so smaller batches do not give a guarantee. They add many more jobs to track.

scenario:
A coding agent keeps a long-term memory store. A user reported the agent failed a release. Excerpts:
memory m-310 (written 41 days ago, source: user message): "To release, run ./scripts/release.sh"
repo history: scripts/release.sh deleted 12 days ago; releases now use `make release`
run log: bash(./scripts/release.sh) -> No such file; agent then recreated the script from its memory of the old contents and ran it
Memory retrieval ranked m-310 first because it matched the task text closely.
stem: Which change to the memory design best prevents this?

options.text: Expire every memory 30 days after it is written, on a schedule, so that stale procedures can no longer be retrieved by any later task.
Store source and time with each memory, verify recalled procedures against current repo state, and update the entry on conflict.
Rank retrieval by similarity blended with write recency, and mark a memory superseded whenever a newer one on the same topic is saved.
Load the repository's README and contributing guide at session start and tell the agent to prefer them over memory whenever the two disagree.

rationale.correct: Memory records what was true when written. Provenance lets the agent decide how much to trust it, a check against the live source finds the contradiction, and updating the entry stops repeat failures.

distractors.A: A fixed age limit also deletes still-valid knowledge and would not catch a procedure changed 3 days after it was written.
distractors.C: Recency of writing is not currency of truth. The repo changed without anyone saving a newer memory, so nothing supersedes m-310 and it still ranks first.
distractors.D: Docs may lag the change, and the agent still acts on the recalled command without checking it. Here it recreated a deleted script from memory instead of reading anything that would reveal the conflict.

scenario:
A shared assistant stores memories in one vector store, retrieved by similarity to the current task. Tenant T-12's session surfaced an entry:
retrieved m-5521 (sim 0.88): "Renewal discount for Globex agreed at 18%, valid to Q3"
m-5521 metadata: {written_by_session: s-0407, tenant: null}
The tool call that retrieved it was memory.search(query="renewal discount", tenant="T-12"), where the tenant argument is filled in by the model; the store ignores unknown filter values. The entry belongs to tenant T-07.
stem: Which TWO changes best close the gap? Select TWO.

options.text: Have the harness inject the tenant from the authenticated session and have the store apply it as a mandatory filter on every query.
Stamp tenant on every write from the session identity, reject writes without one, and quarantine existing entries that have none.
Add an instruction telling the assistant never to disclose another customer's commercial terms in its responses to users.
Strip customer names from memory text before it is stored, so that entries do not identify the account they came from.
Raise the similarity threshold so that only entries closely matching the current task are returned for each query.

rationale.correct: Isolation must be enforced by the harness and store, not by a model-supplied argument. Mandatory filtering on read, plus guaranteed tenant stamping and quarantine on write, close both halves, including the untagged legacy rows.

distractors.C: A prompt rule is probabilistic, and the model has already received the data. The leak is at retrieval, before any disclosure choice.
distractors.D: Removing names hides little: terms, amounts, and context still carry the information, and the entry still crosses the tenant boundary.
distractors.E: A higher threshold only changes which entries cross, and a 0.88 match would pass it anyway. It does not enforce a boundary.

scenario:
Tool-call execution errors rose from 0.4% to 3.1% of agent turns starting Tuesday. Nothing changed in the model version or prompts. Breakdown:
- 94% of failing turns have stop_reason=max_tokens; 6% have end_turn
- failing calls are almost all write_file with long content arguments; short tool calls are unaffected
- Tuesday's cost-saving config change lowered max_tokens from 4096 to 1024 for the agent route
- harness behavior on a JSON parse error: retry the same request up to 3 times
stem: Which diagnosis and fix are best?

options.text: The origin is the output cap, so restore max_tokens for write-heavy calls and treat a max_tokens stop with a partial tool call as incomplete.
The origin is the model producing malformed JSON on long arguments, so add stricter schema instructions and raise the temperature on the retries.
The origin is provider-side flakiness on long outputs, so add exponential backoff between retries and raise the retry limit above three.
The origin is the tool schema for file writes, so split write_file into smaller tools and switch the agent to a larger model.

rationale.correct: Truncation at the limit leaves a partial tool_use input, and the changed max_tokens aligns with the onset and with long-content calls. Raising the limit where needed fixes the cause, and a partial call must not be executed or retried identically.

distractors.B: The outputs are cut off by the limit, not malformed by model error, so stricter instructions do not help and a higher temperature adds variance.
distractors.C: The failures are deterministic for long outputs, and the same request under the same cap truncates again however long it waits.
distractors.D: Splitting tools and changing the model alters several things without touching the 1024-token cap that causes the cut-off.

scenario:
The weekly thumbs-up rate for an assistant fell from 77.8% to 71.6%, and the on-call lead suspects the latest model update. Each week has 10,000 questions, and the weekly thumbs-up rate normally varies by about 0.5 points. Cohort data by question complexity:
         week 1                      week 2
simple   8,000 asked, 85% up         6,000 asked, 86% up
complex  2,000 asked, 49% up         4,000 asked, 50% up
The week-2 jump in complex questions began the day a help-center link to the assistant launched. The model update shipped mid-week 2.
stem: Which TWO first steps best identify the cause of the drop, rather than only confirm it? Select TWO.

options.text: Compare ratings within fixed complexity cohorts across the weeks before attributing the change to the model.
Trace the change in traffic mix to its upstream source, such as the new link's audience and the questions it sends.
Roll back the model update now and hold it off until the thumbs-up rate returns to 77.8%, since the drop followed the update.
Sample 50 low-rated week-2 conversations and edit the prompt to address the most common complaints found in them.
Run a significance test on the 6-point drop to confirm that it is real before deciding what to investigate next.

rationale.correct: Within each cohort the rate is flat or slightly up (85 to 86, 49 to 50), while complex questions went from 20% to 40% of traffic. A cohort comparison shows a mix shift, and tracing it to the link finds the source.

distractors.C: A rollback acts on a coincidence in time. Per-cohort rates did not fall, so it would cost the update's benefits and the aggregate would not return to 77.8%.
distractors.D: Low-rated conversations are mostly the complex ones in either week, so the sample reflects the mix and would send prompt edits after a nonexistent regression.
distractors.E: With 10,000 questions per week and a normal swing of 0.5 points, a 6-point drop is already clearly real, so a test passes without telling a model fault from a population change.

scenario: At 14:05 a finance alert shows that support agents have been issuing refunds above the policy cap since about 13:10. Forty agents share the refund tool, and refunds under the cap are a core support flow that must keep working. The refund API can enforce a hard cap server-side within minutes. Two changes shipped between 13:00 and 13:10: a prompt edit and a tool-schema update, and the cause is not yet known. Rolling either one back means redeploying the agent fleet, about two hours. Full request traces are retained for 4 hours, then reduced to summaries. Each extra hour of the fault issues more refunds that must be clawed back.
stem: Which response sequence is best?

options.text: Disable the refund tool for all 40 agents now, export traces and config while it is off, then restore it once a server-side cap is in place.
Export the traces and config for the window now, then diff the prompt edit against the schema update, ship the fix, and scope the refunds once the cause is confirmed.
Roll back both 13:00-13:10 changes through the fleet pipeline after exporting the traces, then scope the refunds and claw back the excess.
Enforce the hard cap server-side so valid refunds continue, export traces and config for the window, scope the affected refunds, then remediate and root-cause.

rationale.correct: Containment comes first because loss accrues per hour, and a server-side cap works in minutes without stopping valid refunds. Traces drop to summaries after 4 hours, so exporting them before diagnosis protects the evidence needed to scope whom to remediate.

distractors.A: Disabling the tool stops valid under-cap refunds for all 40 agents, a core flow that must keep working, when a server-side cap contains the fault without that cost.
distractors.B: Exporting the traces protects evidence, but diagnosing with the fault still live lets over-cap refunds keep going out for as long as the diff takes, and each extra hour adds clawbacks.
distractors.C: Rollback takes about two hours, so over-cap refunds continue meanwhile, and rolling back two unproven changes is a guess that may not stop the fault. A server-side cap acts in minutes.

scenario:
A tool-schema change broke the address argument for EU locales. It was found after 52 hours through customer tickets. Facts from the review:
- EU is 6% of traffic; EU task success fell from 85% to 40%
- the aggregate task-success alert fires on a drop of 3 points; the aggregate fell by 2.7 points
- normal day-to-day variation in the aggregate is about 1.5 points
- the CI eval set has no EU address cases
stem: Which TWO actions best close the learning loop? Select TWO.

options.text: Alert on task success per locale and key segment, with a minimum-sample guard so that small segments do not page on noise.
Add the failing EU address cases to the CI eval set as permanent regression tests on every tool-schema change.
Lower the aggregate alert threshold from 3 points to 1 point so that a fault of this size would have paged the on-call engineer within a day.
Add a pre-release checklist item requiring the change author to hand-test non-US locales for every tool-schema change and sign off.
Roll out schema changes to a 5% canary and roll back automatically if canary task success drops by the same 3-point aggregate threshold.

rationale.correct: Aggregation diluted a 45-point segment failure to 2.7 points, below the 3-point threshold, so per-segment alerting fixes detection. A permanent regression case turns this incident into a pre-release gate.

distractors.C: A 1-point threshold is inside the 1.5-point normal variation, so it would page falsely on routine days, and it would still be insensitive to smaller segments.
distractors.D: A manual step depends on memory, cannot be verified, and covers only the locales someone thinks to test. It does not catch the next segment or tool that nobody listed.
distractors.E: The canary holds the same 6% EU share, so its aggregate would fall only about 2.7 points, under the 3-point trigger, and the change would be promoted. It has no segment-level view.

scenario:
A support assistant calls the Claude API directly (primary) and fails over to the same model family on a cloud-provider platform (secondary) when the primary returns overloaded or 5xx errors. A per-endpoint circuit breaker opens at 20% errors over 60 seconds. The document-handling step depends on a beta feature that is enabled on the primary. During a primary incident the on-call engineer sees:
primary: 529 overloaded_error on 71% of requests
secondary, requests without the beta header (81% of traffic): 200 OK
secondary, requests with the beta header (19% of traffic): 400 invalid_request_error, feature not supported on this platform
secondary breaker: OPEN after 4 minutes
result: 100% of traffic now receives the static apology page
stem: Which change to the failover design best prevents this outcome?

options.text: Route by capability: fail over only requests the secondary supports, send the rest to a degraded path, and exclude capability-mismatch 400s from breaker health.
Strip the beta header from every failed-over request so the secondary accepts it, and add a notice that document handling differs during failover.
Exclude 4xx responses from breaker accounting, and keep sending the beta-header requests to the primary with exponential backoff until it recovers.
Raise the secondary breaker's threshold to 50% errors over 5 minutes and keep failing over every request, so beta-header 400s no longer open it.

rationale.correct: The secondary works for the 81% of traffic that needs no beta feature; the breaker opened because it counted capability-mismatch 400s as endpoint failures. Routing by required capability keeps the healthy share served and gives the feature-dependent share an intentional degraded path.

distractors.C: Excluding 4xx fixes the breaker, but it sends the 19% back to an endpoint that is failing 71% of requests, with no degraded path.
distractors.B: Silently removing the feature changes the document step's behavior without anyone deciding that is acceptable, and the stripped calls may produce wrong outputs even with a notice.
distractors.D: A looser threshold leaves the 19% of requests still failing with 400s and no degraded path, and it delays opening the breaker when the secondary really is unhealthy.

scenario:
An extraction service runs 64 worker threads that pull from a queue. On HTTP 429 a worker sleeps for the retry-after value (currently 20 to 30 seconds), then retries the same request. Output quality depends on the current model, so requests cannot be moved to another one. The org-level limit is shared with other services, and retry-after reflects when the shared limit will next have capacity. Dashboard at 14:05:
workers asleep on retry-after: 61 of 64
requests sent per minute: 90 (normal: 900)
429 rate: 38% of attempts
queue depth: 2,300 and rising
p99 queue wait: 11 minutes
stem: Which TWO changes best restore throughput without making the rate-limit pressure worse? Select TWO.

options.text: Raise the worker pool from 64 to 256 so that more workers are awake and sending while the others sleep on retry-after.
On 429, requeue the request with a not-before time of retry-after plus jitter, and free the worker so it can take other queued work.
Replace the retry-after wait with exponential backoff starting at 1 second with full jitter, so each worker retries sooner and the fleet recovers capacity faster.
Feed all workers from one shared adaptive limiter that cuts the rate on any 429 and recovers gradually, so the fleet slows and speeds up together.
Cut the pool to a fixed 16 workers so that the fleet can never exceed the rate the shared limit can sustain at its lowest point.

rationale.correct: Sleeping inside a worker turns a short-lived limit into a throughput collapse (90 versus 900 requests per minute), so deferral should happen in the queue and free the worker. A shared adaptive limiter makes the whole fleet slow down together and recover gradually instead of waking in a synchronized herd.

distractors.A: More workers means more concurrent attempts against an already limited org budget, so the 429 rate rises, and most of the new workers will also end up asleep.
distractors.C: Retrying before retry-after probes the limit before capacity exists, so most retries are rejected again. That raises the 429 rate and the pressure on the shared limit.
distractors.E: A fixed small pool throttles below the normal 900 requests per minute even when capacity is free, and it does not adapt when the shared limit moves. It also leaves sleeping workers asleep.

scenario:
A document-digest product launches in 10 days. A load test at the forecast launch peak gave these results:
arrival rate: 12 requests/s (720 per minute)
mean request: 6,000 input tokens, 900 output tokens
mean latency: 18 s
limits: 2,000 requests/min, 3.0M input tokens/min, 800k output tokens/min
observed: 429s on input tokens from the first minute of the peak
40% of the requests are digests that nobody reads for hours, but they arrive during the same peak. Batch API usage is metered separately from these realtime limits. A limit increase takes about 8 weeks to provision, and each digest must cover the whole document.
stem: Which action best fits the situation?

options.text: Request an input-tokens-per-minute increase today and launch on schedule with exponential backoff on 429s until the increase is granted.
Cap client concurrency at 150 so the input-token rate stays under 3.0M per minute, and queue the remainder for the realtime path.
Truncate each document to its first 3,500 input tokens at launch, bringing input to about 2.5M per minute, and widen it after the limit rises.
Move the 40% deferrable digests to the Batch API, which is metered separately, leaving about 2.6M input tokens per minute for the realtime path.

rationale.correct: Input tokens are the binding limit: 12 requests/s x 60 x 6,000 is 4.32M per minute against 3.0M, while requests (36%) and output tokens (about 81%) have headroom. Deferring 40% leaves roughly 2.59M input tokens per minute for the realtime path, under the limit, and needs no provisioning.

distractors.A: The increase takes about 8 weeks against a 10-day launch, and backoff on a limit that is exceeded at steady state only adds retries and queueing.
distractors.B: Concurrency 150 at 18 s supports about 8.3 requests/s against 12 arriving, so the queue grows by about 3.7 requests per second and waits diverge during the peak.
distractors.C: Truncation fits the limit, but each digest must cover the whole document, so every user gets a degraded product to avoid a problem that moving deferrable work removes.

scenario: A queue worker pool admits jobs by request concurrency (a maximum of 40 in flight). Jobs are a mix: about 70% are short chats of roughly 2k input tokens, and 30% are long-document analyses of roughly 45k input tokens. The input-token limit is the binding constraint. Operations notes: 429 bursts appear whenever 5 or more long jobs are in flight together, and the p95 wait for short chats spikes during those bursts because they sit behind retrying long jobs in the same FIFO queue.
stem: Which TWO changes best fix both the 429 bursts and the short-chat wait? Select TWO.

options.text: Admit jobs through a token bucket sized to the input-token limit, charging counted input tokens up front and reconciling to actual usage.
Send long-document jobs to their own lane with a separate queue and smaller concurrency cap, so short chats do not wait behind them.
Raise the request-concurrency cap from 40 to 80 so the shared queue drains faster during the bursts and the backlog clears.
Retry every 429 with exponential backoff and jitter, up to 8 attempts, before failing the job and alerting the on-call engineer.
Cap the request rate at 1,000 requests per minute, which keeps the requests-per-minute counter well under its limit during every burst.

rationale.correct: Concurrency counts requests, but the limit counts tokens, so one long job costs about 22 short ones. Charging admission by tokens aligns the gate with the binding limit, and a separate lane removes head-of-line blocking for short chats.

distractors.C: Doubling request concurrency admits more tokens at once and makes the token limit be exceeded more often.
distractors.D: Backoff recovers individual failures but leaves the mismatched admission gate, and retries from long jobs keep blocking the shared FIFO queue.
distractors.E: A request-rate cap addresses a metric that is not binding; 5 long jobs can still exceed the input-token limit at a low request rate.

scenario:
A multi-turn support agent is rolling out prompt v8, which changes the format of the running summary the agent writes into its own conversation state. The canary assigns v8 to a random 10% of requests. After 6 hours the canary dashboard shows v8 sessions with a higher tool-error rate than v7. Sample log lines:
s-4411 turn1 prompt=v7 ok
s-4411 turn2 prompt=v8 ok
s-4411 turn3 prompt=v7 error: could not parse summary field 'open_items'
s-4412 turn1 prompt=v8 ok
s-4412 turn2 prompt=v7 error: could not parse summary field 'open_items'
About 27% of multi-turn sessions in the canary window contain turns from both versions.
stem: What is the best next step to obtain a valid v7-versus-v8 comparison, given that v7 will not be modified?

options.text: Keep the 10% canary but add a parser that accepts both summary formats, so that v7 and v8 can each read state written by the other version.
Hash the session ID to assign the version for the session's life, key rollback on the same flag, and compare cohorts per session.
Reduce the canary to 1% of requests so that fewer sessions are exposed to mixed versions, while the team investigates the v8 format further.
Treat the error rate as evidence that v8 is worse and roll it back, then redesign the summary format before running another 10% canary.

rationale.correct: Randomizing per request mixes versions inside a session, so v8-versus-v7 comparisons are contaminated and the errors reflect the mix, not v8 itself. Sticky per-session assignment gives a valid cohort comparison and lets rollback act consistently on whole sessions.

distractors.A: A dual-format parser changes v7, which must stay as is, so the canary would compare a patched v7 with v8 and still mix versions inside sessions.
distractors.C: At 1% the number of mixed-version sessions shrinks, but the same contamination remains and the sample becomes too small to detect regressions.
distractors.D: The evidence does not show v8 is worse, since the errors occur on turns that read state written by the other version, so rolling back would discard a candidate on an invalid test.

scenario:
A remote MCP server exposes CRM tools to a multi-tenant assistant. It validates that callers hold a valid token, then calls the CRM backend with one shared service credential that can read every tenant. A security review samples the audit log:
tool=lookup_account tenant=acme principal=svc-mcp-crm
tool=lookup_account tenant=globex principal=svc-mcp-crm
tool=export_contacts tenant=initech principal=svc-mcp-crm
Tenant isolation is currently enforced only by a system prompt telling the model to request records for the current tenant. The team must close the gap before wider rollout.
stem: Which TWO changes best close the gap? Select TWO.

options.text: Accept only tokens issued for this server's own audience, and derive the user and tenant from the validated token.
Forward the caller's inbound access token unchanged to the CRM backend so that the backend sees the end user's identity.
Get tenant-scoped, user-bound downstream credentials by token exchange, enforce tenant authorization per tool call, and log the end user.
Strengthen the system prompt with an explicit rule and worked examples that forbid requesting another tenant's records.
Rotate the shared service credential every 24 hours and move it into a managed secrets store.

rationale.correct: The server must know who is calling (an audience-validated token) and must act with credentials limited to that user's tenant, so the check happens outside the model and the audit log names the real principal. A shared credential with full read access is the confused-deputy gap.

distractors.B: Passing the inbound token through to another service lets a token meant for the MCP server be reused elsewhere, and the backend did not issue or scope it for that purpose.
distractors.D: A prompt rule is advisory and can be bypassed by injection or a model error, so it cannot enforce isolation.
distractors.E: Rotation and a secrets manager protect the credential's storage, but the credential still reads every tenant and the log still shows only the service principal.

scenario:
An enterprise assistant retrieves the top 10 chunks for a query across the whole 6M-chunk index, then removes chunks the user may not read, then sends the rest to Claude. There are 340 overlapping permission groups, and permissions change daily. An evaluation by user type, using questions whose answer lives in documents the user may read:
broad-access users (read about 70% of the corpus): 9.1 of 10 chunks survive the filter, answerable 91%
restricted users (read about 2%): 0.4 of 10 survive, answerable 38%
In 61% of restricted-user failures the model said the information was not available.
stem: Which change best addresses the restricted-user failures?

options.text: Increase the retrieval depth to the top 100 before the permission filter, so that more of the chunks a restricted user may read survive it.
Build a separate index for each of the 340 permission groups, so that every user searches only the content that their group can read.
Apply the permission check as a filter inside the vector search itself, so the top 10 come only from chunks the user may read.
Add a reranker after the permission filter, so that the few chunks which survive are ordered better before they reach Claude.

rationale.correct: Post-filtering lets unreadable chunks occupy the top-k slots, so restricted users receive almost nothing; with 2% readable, even a top 100 yields only about 2 survivors if readability were independent of relevance. Filtering inside the query selects the top results from the readable subset, and permission changes take effect without re-indexing.

distractors.A: At 2% readable, the top 100 yields only a couple of survivors, and the deeper search adds latency for every user.
distractors.B: With 340 overlapping groups, per-group indexes duplicate chunks, and daily permission changes force constant re-indexing and drift.
distractors.D: Reranking reorders what survived, but the problem is that almost nothing survives, so there is little for it to improve.

scenario: A team will move its 40M-chunk retrieval index to a new embedding model. Re-embedding the corpus takes about 9 days. Query and chunk vectors from different embedding models are not comparable in one similarity space. A labeled set of 1,200 queries exists, tagged by query type (conceptual, identifier, multi-hop). The assistant serves live traffic during the migration and must be able to return to the current behavior quickly if quality regresses.
stem: Which TWO practices best manage this migration? Select TWO.

options.text: Build the new index alongside the live one, evaluate it on the labeled queries by query type, and cut over through an alias once no segment regresses.
Re-embed chunks in place in the existing index over the 9 days, and fuse the ranked lists from old-model and new-model queries until the last chunk converts.
Re-embed the 20% of chunks retrieved most often into a second index and query it first, falling back to the old index for anything it misses.
Record the embedding model and index version in each index and trace, and keep the old index and query path until post-cutover monitoring is clean.
Run the labeled set against the new index once, cut over if overall accuracy improves, and keep the old index for a week as a backup.

rationale.correct: A parallel index lets the team test the new space against labeled queries before users see it, and an alias switch makes cutover atomic. Keeping the old index and stamping versions make rollback and diagnosis a configuration change.

distractors.B: In-place overwriting destroys the old vectors, so rollback would mean another 9-day re-embed, and mid-migration the two spaces are mixed inside one index. The fused lists compare scores from incomparable spaces.
distractors.C: A partial index splits the corpus across two incomparable spaces, and identifier and multi-hop queries often hit rarely retrieved chunks, so the result cannot be evaluated or ranked consistently across the corpus.
distractors.E: An overall average can rise while one query type regresses, and a week-long backup does not fix a segment that users already hit. The per-type check is what makes a no-regression cutover decision.

scenario:
A shared 20k-token prefix is eligible for caching. Treat the uncached cost of the prefix as 1.0 per call. A cache write costs 1.25 with the 5-minute lifetime or 2.0 with the 1-hour lifetime; a cache read costs 0.1; each read refreshes the lifetime. Three tenant groups call it differently:
Group 1: bursts of 10 calls two minutes apart, then idle for hours
Group 2: one call every 7 minutes, all day
Group 3: one call every 90 minutes
stem: Which configuration gives the lowest prefix cost per call for each group?

options.text: 5-minute caching for groups 1, 2, and 3, since its write premium is the smaller of the two.
1-hour caching for groups 1, 2, and 3, since a longer lifetime keeps each prefix warm.
1-hour caching for groups 1 and 2, with group 3 left uncached.
5-minute caching for group 1 and 1-hour for group 2, with group 3 left uncached.

rationale.correct: Per call: group 1 with 5-minute is (1.25 + 9 x 0.1)/10 = 0.215 versus 0.29 for 1-hour. Group 2 with 5-minute never hits (1.25, worse than uncached 1.0), while 1-hour is about 0.1 steady state. Group 3 never hits either lifetime, so 1.25 or 2.0 are both worse than 1.0 uncached.

distractors.A: Groups 2 and 3 are called less often than every 5 minutes, so every call is a write at 1.25, more than the uncached 1.0.
distractors.B: Group 3 pays 2.0 per call with no reads, and group 1 pays 0.29 per call against 0.215 on the shorter lifetime.
distractors.C: Group 1 is cheaper at 0.215 on the 5-minute lifetime than at 0.29 on the 1-hour one, because the bursts keep the cache warm and avoid the higher write premium.

scenario:
An agent product spends too much. Per-session analysis over one day (100,000 sessions):
97,000 sessions: average cost 1.0 units, p99.9 of 22 turns, normal completion
3,000 sessions: average cost about 22.5 units, 80% end at the 60-turn cap
The 3% tail accounts for about 41% of spend. Sampled tail traces show the model repeating the same failing tool call, which returns a generic 'error' string. Product leadership has proposed moving the whole fleet to a smaller model.
stem: Which TWO actions best cut cost while protecting quality? Select TWO.

options.text: Move all traffic to a smaller model, since a lower per-token cost applies to every session in the fleet, including the looping tail.
Lower the fleet-wide turn cap from 60 to 30, which stays above the healthy p99.9 of 22 turns, so that no session can burn the full 60.
Add a per-session token and turn budget with repeated-call detection that stops the loop and hands the session off to a person.
After turn 20, restart a long session with a fresh context and a short recap, so that the model is not stuck in its own failing history.
Fix the tool to return a structured, actionable error that says what failed and what to change, then re-measure the tail's share of spend.

rationale.correct: The spend is concentrated in a looping tail, so the effective controls stop loops (budget plus repeated-call detection) and remove the cause (the uninformative tool error that leaves the model retrying). Both leave normal sessions unchanged.

distractors.A: A smaller model trims the 59% of spend that is healthy, at some quality risk, and the tail would still loop at a lower cost per turn.
distractors.B: A cap of 30 stays above healthy sessions, but looping sessions still burn 30 turns of cost and end without a handoff. It limits the loop without stopping it or removing the cause.
distractors.D: A fresh context does not fix the uninformative error, so the model calls the same failing tool again, and it adds a recap step and a turn count to every long session.

scenario:
A report agent must finish in 15 seconds end to end and currently takes 22.4 s. Sequential step timings:
classify (high effort): 5.5 s
retrieve A, B, C (independent of each other, run one after another): 2.1 s, 1.9 s, 2.4 s
draft: 7.0 s
format: 3.5 s
Offline tests show classify and format at low effort take about 1.5 s and 1.0 s with no quality loss. Draft at low effort takes about 3.5 s but drops quality by 4 points, below the release gate.
stem: Which TWO changes meet the 15-second target while keeping the quality gate? Select TWO.

options.text: Run the three retrievals in parallel.
Stream the draft step so that users see text sooner.
Lower the effort level on the classify and format steps.
Cap max_tokens on the draft step so that it finishes sooner.
Lower the effort level on the draft step.

rationale.correct: Parallel retrieval cuts that stage from 6.4 s to 2.4 s (22.4 to 18.4 s), and low effort on classify and format saves a further 6.5 s, for a total of 11.9 s. Neither alone meets 15 s (18.4 s and 15.9 s).

distractors.B: Streaming improves time to first token, but the total time to a complete report does not change.
distractors.D: A lower max_tokens risks max_tokens stops that truncate the draft, and the target is a complete report.
distractors.E: Low effort on the draft would meet the time target together with parallelism but breaks the quality gate by 4 points.

scenario:
A chat feature streams Claude responses over server-sent events, yet users say the answer appears all at once after a long wait. Timings for one request:
API request to first streamed event (measured in the app server): 0.7 s
last streamed event received by the app server: 13.8 s
first byte received by the browser: 14.0 s
browser receives the whole body in one chunk
The app server sits behind a reverse proxy and CDN with default settings. Model, prompt, and effort settings have recently been tuned.
stem: Which change should be made first?

options.text: Lower the effort level and the max_tokens limit so that the model finishes in fewer seconds, since the last event arrives at 13.8 s and the wait looks like generation time.
Disable response buffering and compression on the streaming route at the proxy and CDN, and flush each event as it arrives.
Add a second cache breakpoint so that more of the prefix is served from cache and the first token arrives sooner for every user.
Switch the app server to non-streaming requests and show a progress indicator in the page so that the wait is visible while the answer is prepared.

rationale.correct: The model starts producing tokens at 0.7 s, but nothing reaches the browser until 14.0 s, so an intermediary is buffering the whole response. Turning off buffering on that route restores incremental delivery of what is already being streamed.

distractors.A: Generation does take about 13 s, but the model emits its first event at 0.7 s, so a shorter answer would still reach the browser in one chunk after the buffer flushes. It also changes content.
distractors.C: TTFT at the model is already 0.7 s, and caching cannot remove a 13-second delay introduced after the app server.
distractors.D: Non-streaming makes the wait the full generation time by design. A progress indicator hides nothing about the 14 s, and the app server already receives events promptly, so the fault is downstream.

scenario:
A claims-processing agent runs under a customer contract that forbids retaining prompt or completion text anywhere outside the customer's own tenant. A platform audit of the shared tracing backend found this span attribute on 100% of spans, retained 30 days:
span: agent.turn  attrs: gen_ai.prompt.text="<full prompt>" gen_ai.completion.text="<full completion>" tool.args="<json>"
The content attributes must be removed, yet on-call engineers still need to diagnose agent loops that stall, retry, or pick wrong tools. Reproduction can use synthetic fixtures.
stem: Which TWO telemetry changes best preserve debuggability within the contract? Select TWO.

options.text: Keep the content attributes but encrypt them with a platform-held key and cut retention to 7 days, so only on-call staff can decrypt them in incidents.
Record per turn: stop_reason, token counts, tool name, argument-validation result, tool latency and error class, retry count, and the request ID.
Run an entity redactor over prompt and completion text to tokenize names and policy numbers, then keep the remaining text for 30 days.
Tag spans with prompt-template ID, version, and a hash of the rendered prompt, so an engineer can replay the matching template on a synthetic fixture.
Capture content only on spans that end in an error, since failed turns are the ones engineers read, and drop text from successful turns.

rationale.correct: Structural metadata and template identity explain loop behavior (where it stalled, which tool failed, which template version) without any customer text leaving the tenant. A hash lets engineers group identical inputs and replay a matching synthetic fixture.

distractors.A: Encryption and shorter retention still retain the text outside the customer's tenant, which the contract forbids.
distractors.C: Entity redaction is incomplete, and the remaining prompt and completion text is still retained outside the tenant, which the contract forbids.
distractors.E: Error spans still carry customer text, so the contract is still violated, and the stalls and retries the team needs to diagnose are often in turns that end normally.

scenario:
A multi-tenant assistant has a 9,000-token system prompt: a 2,000-token tenant-specific block first, then a 7,000-token shared policy block, then the conversation. A cache breakpoint is set at the end of the system prompt. Cache entries expire if unused for a few minutes. Last week's dashboard:
cache_creation_input_tokens: 71% of cacheable tokens
cache_read_input_tokens: 6% of cacheable tokens
median gap between requests for the same tenant: 11 min; for the fleet as a whole: 1.4 s
prompt text per tenant is byte-identical across requests; deploys were unchanged this week
stem: The team needs reads to dominate without adding per-tenant traffic or rewording any prompt text. What is the best change?

options.text: Send a lightweight keep-alive request per tenant every four minutes, so each tenant's cached prefix stays warm between that tenant's real requests.
Place the 7,000-token shared policy block first and the breakpoint right after it, so all tenants read one prefix requested every 1.4 s.
Add a second breakpoint after the tenant block, so the 2,000-token tenant prefix is cached on its own and read on that tenant's next request.
Disable caching for this prompt, since a 6% read share means the write premium costs more than the reads can recover at this traffic.

rationale.correct: Caching matches a stable prefix from the start. Because the tenant block comes first, each tenant's prefix is unique and its entry expires during the 11-minute gap. Putting the shared block first lets all tenants hit the same prefix, which is requested every 1.4 s fleet-wide.

distractors.A: Keep-alive pings add a paid request per tenant every four minutes, which violates the no-added-traffic constraint, and the structural cause (a unique prefix per tenant) remains.
distractors.C: The 11-minute gap exceeds the entry lifetime, so the tenant-only entry expires before the next request. The 7,000 shared tokens also still sit behind a tenant-unique prefix and cannot be shared across tenants.
distractors.D: Disabling caching forgoes the large saving available from the shared 7,000 tokens, and the low read share is a prompt-layout defect, not evidence that caching cannot pay off.

scenario:
A document-processing service shipped a prompt change in week 2. Weekly data:
               tasks    spend    success   tool calls/task   output tokens/request
week 1       100,000   $4,000    92%         2.1                405
week 2       140,000   $7,280    91%         3.0                398
A marketing campaign raised volume in week 2. Current alerts: page if daily spend exceeds 2x the 30-day average; ticket if success rate drops below 88%. Neither fired.
stem: Which TWO alerts would have caught this change earliest while staying quiet on legitimate volume growth? Select TWO.

options.text: Alert when daily spend exceeds 1.5x the 30-day average, so the next jump of this size would fire on its own.
Alert when cost per successful task rises past a set percentage over a trailing baseline, by prompt version.
Alert when average output tokens per request rises, since output tokens drive most of the cost growth in this service.
Alert when p95 tool calls per task shifts above its baseline for the same prompt version.
Alert when the thumbs-down rate rises, since users notice a worse experience before any other metric moves.

rationale.correct: Cost per successful task is $0.0435 in week 1 and $0.0571 in week 2 (+31%) while total spend rose 82% mostly from volume; normalizing by successful work isolates the behavioral change. Tool calls per task rose from 2.1 to 3.0 with flat output tokens, so loop depth is the leading indicator.

distractors.A: A lower fixed threshold on total spend would fire on every campaign and seasonal volume rise, so it trades missed detection for false pages.
distractors.C: Output tokens per request are flat (405 to 398), so this signal would not have moved; the extra cost came from more tool calls.
distractors.E: Success held at 91-92% and nothing in the data shows user dissatisfaction; thumbs-down is a lagging, sparse signal and does not attribute the cost change.

scenario: A support assistant handles 50,000 conversations per day. An online judge scores 2% of them (1,000 per day) for groundedness. The SLO is 97% grounded over 30 days. After a bad week the team wants a page within one hour of any real slip. Proposal: page whenever the hourly judged-groundedness SLI falls below 94%. Other signals computed on every request: schema-validation failure rate, refusal rate, citation-missing rate, tool error rate. In past slips, citation-missing and schema-failure rates moved within minutes.
stem: Which alerting design is best?

options.text: Page on the hourly judged SLI as proposed, but require two consecutive hours below 94%, so that a single noisy hour of sampling cannot trigger a page.
Raise judge sampling to 100% of traffic so each hourly SLI rests on about 2,000 judged conversations and can page precisely within the hour.
Move the judged SLI to a weekly window, which gives enough samples to estimate it precisely and avoids hourly false alarms from sampling noise.
Page on the full-population proxies, run the judged SLI as a 24-hour burn ticket, and raise judge sampling whenever a proxy moves.

rationale.correct: At 2% sampling the hour holds about 42 judged conversations, so a 97% rate has a 95% interval of roughly ±5.2 points, wider than the whole 3-point budget; a 94% hourly threshold fires on noise and misses real slips. Proxies are measured on every request and can page within minutes; the 24-hour window has about 1,000 samples (±1.1 points), and a proxy trigger can raise sampling to confirm.

distractors.A: Two consecutive hours (about 84 samples) still carry roughly ±3.7 points of noise, and a page can come no sooner than two hours into a slip, missing the one-hour goal.
distractors.B: Judging every conversation costs about 50 times the current judge spend for a quality check, and is unnecessary when full-population proxies can page and a daily window is precise enough.
distractors.C: A weekly window is precise but delays detection by days, which contradicts the one-hour goal and lets a regression burn most of the 30-day budget.

scenario:
A retention policy keeps 100% of failed traces and a 5% random sample of successful traces. A support agent's retained traces by workflow in one day:
workflow            failed kept   successes kept
order-status           640            3,000
refund-reissue         520            1,900
address-change         150            2,100
gift-card-redeem         9                6
An analyst ranked workflows by retained failure share and flagged gift-card-redeem (60%) as the top issue.
Past fixes brought a workflow's failure rate down to about the fleet-wide rate, and the team can fix one workflow this sprint.
stem: Which analysis and next step are best supported?

options.text: Investigate gift-card-redeem first: even after reweighting its failure rate is the highest at about 7%, so it is the most broken workflow in the fleet and the best target.
Investigate order-status first: it has the most retained failures (640), so fixing it would remove the most failed traces from the fleet and the most customer pain.
Investigate refund-reissue first: reweighted by 1/0.05 its rate is about 1.35% versus 0.93% fleet-wide, about 160 excess failures against under 10 for gift-card.
Stop the analysis: the retained sample is skewed, so no workflow-level rate can be trusted until retention is changed to sample all traces uniformly.

rationale.correct: Retained rates are biased because failures are over-kept 20x. Reweighting successes gives true counts (refund 38,520 traces, order-status 60,640). Bringing refund-reissue to the fleet rate removes about 160 failures, versus about 75 for order-status and about 8 for gift-card-redeem.

distractors.A: Gift-card-redeem has the highest reweighted rate (about 7%, from 9 failures in roughly 129 traces), but bringing it to the fleet rate removes under 10 failures, so it is the wrong use of this sprint. The 60% figure is a retention artifact.
distractors.B: Raw retained failure counts follow workflow volume. Order-status has a 1.06% rate, so bringing it to the fleet rate removes only about 75 failures, fewer than refund-reissue.
distractors.D: The known sampling probabilities make unbiased reweighting possible, so rates can be recovered without a new policy; waiting delays the diagnosis.

scenario:
Two agent versions are compared on 1,000 production traces each. Version 2 is routed the harder tickets by a classifier.
                simple tickets        complex tickets        overall
v1             16 / 800 fail (2.0%)   40 / 200 fail (20.0%)   56 / 1,000 (5.6%)
v2              3 / 200 fail (1.5%)  128 / 800 fail (16.0%)  131 / 1,000 (13.1%)
A dashboard flags v2 as 'failure rate more than doubled'.
stem: Which TWO steps best establish whether v2 is actually worse? Select TWO.

options.text: Drop the complex tickets from the comparison, since they are hard for any version and mostly add noise to the totals.
Replay one fixed set of tickets, stratified by complexity, through both versions.
Compare the versions on average tokens per trace, since cost per trace reveals whether v2 is working harder than v1.
Compare versions within ticket-complexity strata, or after reweighting both to one complexity mix.
Roll back v2 immediately, because the overall failure rate more than doubled and continued production exposure is the larger risk.

rationale.correct: Overall rates are confounded by routing: v2 receives 80% complex tickets versus 20% for v1, and v2 is lower within both strata (1.5% vs 2.0% and 16% vs 20%). Stratified comparison or a replay on a fixed, balanced set separates version effect from case mix.

distractors.A: Complex tickets are the bulk of v2's traffic and carry the highest failure rates; removing them hides the cases that matter most.
distractors.C: Token counts say nothing about which version fails more on comparable tickets and do not address the mix difference.
distractors.E: The stratified rates show v2 failing less on both groups, so a rollback would remove a better version based on a mix artifact.

scenario:
A CI gate blocks a prompt change if the pass rate on a 200-case regression suite falls below 90%. Five consecutive runs on the unchanged main branch (single trial per case, sampling enabled):
run 1: 91.0%   run 2: 88.5%   run 3: 92.5%   run 4: 89.0%   run 5: 91.5%
Developers now re-run failed gates until green. A teammate proposes lowering the threshold to 87%. A past regression cost 3 points on one safety-relevant category.
stem: Which change best makes the gate reliable?

options.text: Run several trials per case, gate on the paired difference from a same-job baseline plus a noise margin, and add per-category floors.
Lower the threshold to 87% so unchanged code stops failing, and add a separate 95% floor on the safety category from the single-trial results.
Set temperature to 0 and fix the sampling seed for gate runs so results become repeatable, and keep the 90% threshold on the pass rate.
Gate on the mean of three consecutive runs against the 90% threshold, so the single-run noise averages out before the pass or fail decision.

rationale.correct: Run-to-run swings of about 4 points (88.5 to 92.5) exceed the 3-point regression the team must catch. Multiple trials and a paired comparison against the baseline shrink the noise, and category floors protect the critical slice that an aggregate average hides.

distractors.B: An 87% threshold would still pass a real 3-point aggregate drop from about 90.5%. A 95% floor on a small category scored with one trial per case is itself noisy, so the gate would flap on unchanged code.
distractors.C: Temperature 0 does not guarantee deterministic outputs and measures behavior unlike production sampling, so it hides variance instead of measuring it. A fixed 90% line also leaves no margin.
distractors.D: The five-run mean is 90.5%, only 0.5 above the line, so even a three-run mean fails unchanged code a meaningful share of the time. It still compares to an absolute line, not a paired baseline, and hides category-level regressions.

scenario:
A team gates model migrations on a 600-case golden set. Audit results:
subset                          cases   pass rate on last 6 releases
saturated (always passed)         140        100%
near-duplicate clusters            90        (31 clusters, 3 variants each)
long-document tickets               0        -
Production mix: long-document tickets are 22% of traffic and were behind the last two incidents. Headline pass rate has been 97-98% for a year, so it no longer separates releases.
stem: Which TWO changes best restore the suite's validity? Select TWO.

options.text: Fill the long-document gap by asking the model under evaluation to generate synthetic long-document tickets and reference answers, then add them as cases.
Raise the pass threshold from 95% to 99% so the headline discriminates between releases again without changing any cases.
Move saturated cases to a smoke tier outside the headline, and count each near-duplicate cluster once in the release metric.
Add labeled long-document cases sampled from production, held out from tuning, as their own category with a floor.
Delete the failing cases from the last six releases, since persistent failures are likely mislabeled and drag the headline score down.

rationale.correct: Saturated and duplicated cases inflate the headline without information, and the suite has no coverage for the traffic slice behind the incidents. Re-weighting for independent cases and adding held-out production-derived long-document cases addresses saturation and coverage.

distractors.A: Cases generated by the model being evaluated share its blind spots and style, so they under-represent real failures and tilt results toward the model.
distractors.B: A higher threshold on the same inflated 97-98% metric still leaves a headline made of saturated and duplicate cases, and gives no coverage of long documents.
distractors.E: The suite's problem is too few failures, not too many; deleting failing cases removes signal and would raise the score further.

scenario:
A judge labels support answers pass/fail. On a 300-answer set labeled by humans (270 human-pass, 30 human-fail), the judge scored:
                 judge pass   judge fail
human pass          262            8
human fail           23            7
Raw agreement is 89.7%, above the team's 85% bar. In production about 10% of answers fail, and failures are what the judge exists to catch. A second check: re-running the judge with the two answers in swapped order on 100 pairwise items changed the verdict on 18.
stem: Which TWO next steps best address the judge's quality? Select TWO.

options.text: Rewrite the rubric with failure-mode anchors from the 23 missed failures, then re-score a fresh labeled set not used for tuning.
Report agreement by class and sign off if pass-class agreement (262/270, 97%) clears the bar, since failures are rare in production traffic.
Report recall on human-fail cases (7/30 = 23%) and kappa (about 0.26), and re-measure on a set oversampling human-fail answers.
Add the 23 missed failures from the 300 labeled answers to the judge prompt as few-shot examples, and re-report agreement on the same 300.
Run the judge twice per answer with the order swapped and keep only agreeing verdicts, since the 18% flip rate shows the verdicts are unstable.

rationale.correct: With 90% passes, accuracy is dominated by the majority class: the judge catches only 7 of 30 real failures (23%) and kappa is about 0.26. Per-class metrics on a failure-rich sample show the real quality, and a rubric revised from observed misses must be validated on fresh labeled data.

distractors.B: Pass-class agreement says nothing about catching failures, which is what the judge exists to do, and it is inflated by the 90% pass prevalence. The 18% verdict flip on swapped order is also a position bias.
distractors.D: Few-shot examples taken from the 300 answers leak the test items into the prompt, so re-scoring the same set measures memorization and would overstate quality on unseen traffic.
distractors.E: Order swapping targets position bias in pairwise mode, while the pass/fail misses are systematic (the same failure types accepted in both orders), and discarding disagreements removes the hardest cases.

scenario:
A team compares candidate model B against current model A using a judge from a provider alias that was upgraded to a new judge version on the same day candidate B shipped to the eval. Mean judge scores (1-5):
                                   old judge   new judge
frozen anchor set (120 outputs, human mean 3.6)    3.7      4.1
model A outputs (last month)                  3.8      4.2
model B outputs (today)                        n/a      4.4
The report says 'B improves quality by 0.6 over A last month's 3.8'.
stem: What is the best way to evaluate whether B improved?

options.text: Subtract the 0.4 anchor-set shift from B's score and report B at 4.0, since the shift is a measured offset between the two judge versions.
Hold the comparison until the provider documents what changed in the judge, since scores from an unexplained version cannot support a decision.
Report the 0.6 gain with a bootstrap confidence interval over outputs, since sampling error is the main risk when comparing two models' means.
Score A and B in one run with the same judge version, re-score the anchor set as a check, and report the within-judge difference.

rationale.correct: Scores from different judge versions are not on one scale: the anchor set moved from 3.7 to 4.1 with no change in the outputs. Comparing A and B within one judge version in one run removes the drift; the anchor re-score documents it. The within-judge gain is about 0.2, not 0.6.

distractors.A: A single global offset assumes the shift is uniform across output quality and categories. That is unverified, and 4.0 versus 3.8 is still a cross-version comparison.
distractors.B: The drift is already measurable from the anchor set, and a same-version comparison is valid without any explanation from the provider, so waiting only delays the decision.
distractors.C: An interval measures sampling error, but the 0.6 is mostly a systematic judge-version shift (the anchor set moved 0.4 with identical outputs). A tighter interval around a biased gap is still biased.

scenario:
A team A/B tests a new answer prompt (arm B) against the current one (arm A). Escalation can fall when a bot deflects users who would otherwise reach a human. Results after two weeks:
                       arm A     arm B
conversations         40,000    40,000
feedback widget shown  yes       yes (more prominent in arm B layout)
feedback given         3.8%      6.1%
thumbs-up among given  81%       76%
escalated to human in 24h   9.4%    8.1%
The product lead says arm B 'lost 5 points of thumbs-up' and wants to cancel.
stem: What is the best interpretation and next step?

options.text: Cancel arm B: thumbs-up fell from 81% to 76% on about 2,440 responses versus 1,520 in arm A, so the larger sample makes the gap statistically reliable.
Treat feedback as confounded by response rate; compare escalation and repeat contact over all assigned conversations and read a random sample.
Keep arm B because escalations fell from 9.4% to 8.1%, and set the feedback data aside since the widget layout differs between arms.
Rerun the test and compute thumbs-up over only the first 1,000 feedback events in each arm, which equalizes the sample sizes.

rationale.correct: Arm B's widget raised the response rate (3.8% to 6.1%), so the extra respondents are a different, likely more critical population; thumbs-up among respondents is not comparable. An outcome measured on all assigned users, plus an unbiased sampled review, avoids the selection effect.

distractors.A: A larger sample gives a tighter estimate, but a more prominent widget changes who responds, so the 5-point drop mixes a prompt effect with a population effect.
distractors.C: A lower escalation rate can come from deflecting users who needed a human, so it needs a check on resolution quality; ignoring feedback entirely discards signal rather than correcting its bias.
distractors.D: Taking the first 1,000 events per arm still selects only respondents and adds time-of-test bias; it does not remove the selection effect.

scenario: A document-extraction pipeline auto-accepts records when model confidence is at least 0.9 (about 85% of volume) and routes the rest to human review. Reviewers correct fields on the routed records, and customers report errors days later through a ticket system. The team has no live ground truth and wants an online accuracy measure it can trust. Offline accuracy was 96%.
stem: Which TWO online measures best fit? Select TWO.

options.text: Track the mean model confidence score per day, since a falling mean signals that accuracy has degraded in production.
Human-label a random weekly sample of auto-accepted records, independent of confidence, and report field accuracy with an interval.
Track the reviewers' correction rate on the routed queue, since it shows how often the model's outputs are wrong when it is unsure of them.
Track customer-reported corrections per 1,000 accepted records, bucketed by extraction date so late reports update earlier weeks.
Track the schema-validation pass rate of extracted records, since a falling rate signals that extraction quality is degrading.

rationale.correct: The auto-accepted 85% has no human check, so a random audit of that group gives an unbiased accuracy estimate where errors are least visible. Downstream corrections cover all accepted records and add a trailing signal, provided reports are attributed back to the extraction date.

distractors.A: Mean confidence is the model's self-report and can stay high while accuracy drops, so it is unchecked against ground truth.
distractors.C: The review queue holds only low-confidence records, so its correction rate describes the hard minority and says nothing about the auto-accepted majority.
distractors.E: Schema validity tests format, not whether field values are right; accuracy can fall while records still validate.

scenario:
A support assistant streams replies to a web widget token by token. A PII redactor scans the completed reply and, on a hit, replaces the stored message and tells the widget to remove the text. Audit excerpt from a customer complaint:
12:04:01.120 stream start req_88
12:04:03.410 chunk delivered to widget: '...your card ending 4417, billing address 22 Alder...'
12:04:05.900 stream end
12:04:06.350 redactor: 2 findings, stored message replaced
12:04:06.360 widget event: message_redacted
The customer had already captured the text on screen. Product will not drop streaming, because the first-token target is under one second.
stem: Which change best closes the exposure while keeping most of the streaming benefit?

options.text: Make the redactor finish within 100 ms of stream end, which shrinks the interval before the widget removes text that was already shown.
Scan the stream as it forms and release text only after a short lookahead window is checked, holding the stream while a finding is open.
Add a system-prompt rule not to output card or address details, test it against 200 adversarial prompts, and keep the completed-reply redactor as backstop.
Disable streaming only for conversations that an intent classifier labels account-related, and keep token-level streaming for all the rest.

rationale.correct: The leak happened at 12:04:03, while the stream was still running, so any control that acts after text has been delivered is too late. A small hold-back buffer lets the filter act before release and costs a few hundred milliseconds of extra delay rather than all of the streaming benefit.

distractors.A: Text was visible for about three seconds before the stream even ended; a faster post-hoc scan still runs after delivery and cannot unsee the screenshot.
